Date: 11-Feb-26
Reference Number: 19167843
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Services
Buyer Role: Head of Enterprise Architecture
Purpose: Enterprise AI Strategy
Question Asked: My framework uses a 'Build vs. Buy vs. Federate' logic. Specifically for the 'Federate' path, do you see a dominant design pattern emerging for the 'Orchestrator of Orchestrators'? Am I risking technical debt by trying to centralize orchestration (e.g., in ServiceNow) rather than allowing a looser, mesh-like handoff between M365 and Workday agents?

I'm looking to fill in the gaps of the strategy and strengthen it.

 

This document outlines the strategic framework for the organization’s transition from ad-hoc AI experimentation to operational, industrialized scale. We are adopting a Microsoft-First, Federated Intelligence Model that definitively rejects the concept of building a monolithic "AI Brain" or centralized data lake for all intelligence. Instead, we are building a unified user experience powered by a distributed network of specialized, domain-aware intelligence.


In this model, Microsoft 365 Copilot serves as the universal "Pane of Glass"—the single, consistent interface where employees interact with enterprise intelligence across all surfaces. However, the underlying logic, data, and reasoning remain federated: routine, cross-functional tasks are orchestrated via Copilot Studio; complex, high-compute engineering flows through Microsoft Foundry; and deep, domain-specific authority remains with Digital Platforms & Enterprise Applications (e.g., ITSM, HCM, Finance).


This strategy maximizes business value by leveraging our existing Microsoft ecosystem investment while respecting the "System of Record" authority of our enterprise platforms. It ensures speed to market, robust security inheritance, and a measurable Return on Investment (ROI) by preventing duplicate engineering efforts.
Analyst Name: Saikat Ray
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To develop a comprehensive enterprise AI strategy that considers the integration of Microsoft M365 Copilot, Azure AI Foundry, and other potential tools to ensure flexibility and scalability in AI deployment.

Summary:
- The discussion focused on developing an enterprise AI strategy, with the customer already utilizing Microsoft tools like M365 Copilot and Azure AI Foundry.
- The customer expressed uncertainty about relying solely on Microsoft tools due to potential limitations and sought advice on a strategic approach.
- The Gartner expert suggested a federated approach over a monolithic AI system to avoid technical debt and maintain flexibility.
- The expert highlighted the benefits of leveraging existing systems and emphasized the importance of a system of record for retaining authority.
- Concerns were raised about using Copilot Studio as a default orchestrator due to its limitations in handling complex workflows.
- The expert recommended considering Azure Foundry for model orchestration but noted it may not be suitable for process orchestration.
- Mike Warren suggested using Azure Data Factory and Power Automate for orchestration, emphasizing security integration and deployment capabilities.
- The customer inquired about when to enable AI features in SaaS tools like Workday and Salesforce, seeking guidance to avoid unnecessary hype.
- The expert advised against tightly coupling AI agents with systems of record, recommending a federated strategy for flexibility.
- The discussion included examples of deploying orchestration agents across multiple platforms, with a focus on maintaining a single orchestration layer.
- The expert suggested using a design layer for process orchestration, considering tools like Camunda or Temporal for durable execution.
- The importance of governance, control tower approaches, and observability in managing AI agents was emphasized.
- The customer planned to revise their strategy based on the discussion and schedule a follow-up meeting for further review.

Purpose: Data Observability
Question Asked: Cost and data-quality optimization for observability (logs & metrics), with a focus on GCP and ServiceNow event noise.

-   How should we design and govern log/metric collection so that we only collect “must-have” telemetry while maintaining sufficient visibility for SRE/operations and incident response?
-   What are Gartner-recommended practices and concrete examples for:
    -   Log severity filtering?
    -   Defining “golden signals/metrics” and standard telemetry baselines across heterogeneous technologies?
-   How are other large enterprises practically managing and reducing observability spend while also reducing noise and improving data quality for AI/analytics?

Customer’s explicit questions:
1.  Best practices for what logs “must” be collected (e.g., ERROR vs INFO).
2.  Any ready-made log pattern-   /filters that can be ignored for GCP services & applications/compute.
-   How peers manage cost for logs/metrics from observability platforms.
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: I suggested this email be sent to the client:

Hello,

It was great speaking with you today. I wanted to send you a few follow-up thoughts. At the bottom of this email, I included links to some helpful research.

As we discussed, one way to manage your log telemetry volume is to focus on capturing the logs most valuable for observability. These are typically logs at the FATAL, ERROR, and WARNING levels. While INFO logs can provide important context for root-cause analysis, it’s best to filter and retain only those INFO logs that contain relevant fields or patterns, rather than ingesting all INFO logs by default. Your GCP telemetry pipeline can filter on multiple dimensions (e.g., severity, service, endpoint) and structured fields, allowing you to keep only what is meaningful. This approach works best when your services use structured logging, as it enables the pipeline to match on specific fields. This way, you get the diagnostic detail you need while keeping overall volume and cost under control.

I have included a link below on centralized log management and monitoring.

Following up on your question about how to approach golden signals and practical guidance on what to measure, here are my recommendations.

Use the four Golden Signals as the foundational baseline for monitoring system health. As we discussed, these include Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation. This baseline will help IT operations shift away from reactive, infrastructure‑focused monitoring and toward proactive, business‑centric observability.

Implement the Golden Signals across all business‑critical applications so that each service inherits the same baseline without requiring custom definitions from scratch. These signals also provide the starting point for establishing your Service‑Level Indicators (SLIs) and Service‑Level Objectives (SLOs).

For example:
Availability and Traffic: percentage of successful requests based on HTTP status codes, often with targets such as 99.9 percent over 30 days
Latency: span or request duration using p95 and p99 thresholds, such as a p95 under 500 ms
Error Rate: spans or requests that record errors, enriched with exception details to identify bottlenecks
Saturation: CPU, memory, thread usage, and queue depth to identify resource constraints before users feel the impact

For mobile and front‑end applications, traditional backend metrics often miss what customers experience. If you are using Real User Monitoring (RUM), I recommend a parallel set of Mobile RUM Golden Signals that capture load times, transaction success rates, frontend latency, session duration, abandonment, geographic or network variance, and frustration indicators such as repeated rapid inputs.

Guidance Framework for Deploying Centralized Log Management and Monitoring
Log data is essential for diagnosing issues; however, distributed architectures, such as cloud technologies, microservices and containerization, complicate centralized log management and monitoring. This guide offers best practices for effectively managing cloud, system and application logs.
D.B. Cummings | Dylan Roberts

Reference Architecture Brief: Best Practice Framework for Observability and Incident Response
Siloed observability and incident response impede proactive prevention and swift resolution. This research outlines a best practice framework for IT operations specialists to unify telemetry, reduce tool sprawl, surface actionable insights, and automate incident remediation.
D.B. Cummings | Dylan Roberts | Tyler Cheney

As a reminder, BTI does not send the research recommendations directly to prospective clients. Instead we are sending these to you as the main point of contact between Gartner and Sujithkumar Chandra. Please utilize them during your sales process.

Thank you,

Regards,
D.B. Cummings
Sr Director Analyst

Analyst Name: Saikat Ray
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To identify and implement effective security hardening strategies for RPA automation at the University of Amsterdam, focusing on risk mitigation, segregation, and secure orchestration.

Summary:
- Max Cornel explained the university’s challenge: integrating RPA securely without undermining business case viability or operational efficiency. Max highlighted extensive internal security policies and the difficulty of balancing robust controls with workable automation.
- Saikat outlined common RPA risks, including cross-zone access, segregation of duties, privilege concentration, and bot identity impersonation.
- Saikat recommended enforcing hard network boundaries, isolating bot execution in dedicated zones, and using micro-segmentation for access control.
- He emphasized adopting a zero trust strategy for bots, requiring individual bot accounts, no shared credentials, and conditional access policies.
- Saikat advised certificate-based authentication for bot communications and unique bot IDs for auditability and traceability.
- He stressed secure credential management, including encryption at rest and in transit, use of vaults, and prohibiting local credential storage.
- Saikat recommended hardening bot machines with endpoint controls, no local admin rights, application allow-listing, and disabling peripheral access.
- Max confirmed many of these controls were implemented but expressed concern about backend zoning and process orchestration.
- Saikat clarified that tasks should be split among separate bots per zone, with orchestration managed by a secure, enterprise-grade orchestrator.
- He described the orchestrator’s role in state management, security enforcement, and event-driven control, separate from bot runtime logic.
- Saikat advocated for robust observability and runtime monitoring, using telemetry and audit logs to detect anomalies and ensure compliance.
- He concluded with best practices: API-first architecture, strict change management, ID lifecycle controls, and regular entitlement reviews, offering to share relevant Gartner research.

Key takeaways:
- Saikat Ray will share security research documents around bots with Maarten Emons.  
- Saikat Ray will include points discussed during the call in the shared materials.

Date: 2-Feb-26
Reference Number: 19242526
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Manufacturing
Buyer Role: Head of Infrastructure and/or IT Operations
Purpose: Company Store Setup
Question Asked: Paul Perpich is seeking to streamline the purchasing process for company equipment, such as headsets and monitors, by implementing a company store. He aims to provide a better interface for users to select supported items and ensure budget holder approval. The goal is to gain better control over purchases and avoid issues with varied and oversized equipment. Questions are - What are the best practices for setting up a company store that efficiently manages purchaser and approver roles? How can we ensure the store provides a seamless user experience while maintaining control over equipment types and sizes?
Analyst Name: Mike Lowndes
Discussion Summary: WR sent. Paul Perpich is seeking to streamline the purchasing process for company equipment, such as headsets and monitors, by implementing a company store. 
He aims to provide a better interface for users to select supported items and ensure budget holder approval. 
The goal is to gain better control over purchases and avoid issues with varied and oversized equipment. 

My understanding of the question: this is an *internal store* for staff only to buy approved items.

It's not clear whether your company buys stock and then resells it internally, or interfaces between your buyers and the vendor direct, or a mix of both. 
	1. Some suppliers provide 'staff portals' (B2B2X we call them), or 'employee purchase programs'  to enable your staff to purchase online. This may be an option, or an option used for certain categories. 
	2. Some procurement / asset management systems enable this e.g. SAP Ariba, Coupa, Workday Procurement. You'd need to talk to a procurement analyst for more info on these solutions.  Servicenow has also extended into this space with 'Servicenow Catalog'.
	3. Internal ecommerce shop. It would need to be integrated into the procurement system to get the catalog details and price - and/or - integrated to the 3rd party supplier(s) for the same. This latter technique is technically uses 'enterprise marketplace' software. 

Questions are - What are the best practices for setting up a company store that efficiently manages purchaser and approver roles? 

Use a B2B oriented platform: Purchaser and approvals roles are a standard component of ecommerce platforms build for business to business. They come with these roles out of the box, including notifications etc, budget restrictions and buying limits. An open source example would be Shopware. Spryker is a more enterprise solution. Bigcommerce is a SaaS solution. Salesforce B2B Commerce can also be configured for this. The roles can be imported from an ERP or staff directory service.

How can we ensure the store provides a seamless user experience while maintaining control over equipment types and sizes?

Types and sizes are set in the catalog, which you will have control of unless controlled by your supplier (see above). 'Seamless user experience' is more about UI design than anything technical, but UI design tends to be neglected on internal projects, so my recommendation is not to neglect it. 
Appropriate integration - such as staff info: role, dept, access level etc is imported, and single-sign-on is enabled e.g. Octa. 

Paul Perpich has experienced challenges with the current company store setup, particularly with CDW, which did not fit their needs despite being a specialized provider.
…. the setup has been problematic, especially regarding purchaser and approver roles, leading to a pause in the project. Paul is considering revisiting Amazon or finding a smoother solution.

CDW is a software development house, they make money from creating bespoke software. Instead use off-the-shelf ecommerce software and hire an implementation / integration company to ensure it is configured to your needs. 

They initially considered Amazon for a branded store but returned to CDW after changes in the project team. 

I can't help with Amazon Business: I have no idea if this is a good fit or not: as above it depends how you source the things you sell to your staff.

Purpose: ServiceNow Models in Healthcare
Question Asked: Client would like to know if we have information on successful support models (in healthcare) for ServiceNow?

Analyst Name: Faith Adams
Discussion Summary: Hello Nickie 





        I am sorry we were unable to connect today at our scheduled time. I know Mondays can be hectic! In the meantime, though, I did want to provide an abbreviated answer to your question about ServiceNow Models in Healthcare.

I am going to do my best to outline what I have seen in our industry. I also would suggest a call w/ the ServiceNow lead analysts about what other regulated industries may be doing, too. I always recommend seeing what others are doing, too, to see the art of what may be possible. 

Generally speaking, I am seeing more of a move to more of a centralized structure with tiers then. This can vary at times based on factors like the size of an organization, complexity, change acceptance and fatigue levels, and nature of clinical integration. 

Here is some additional info to consider first: the degree of DIY/self-service and automation goals of your org. This may also dictate the model you aim for. 

Continuous improvement is also critical. Will you use analytics and reporting and other feedback to drive continued change (including change of the model)? 

As far as the main models I see: 

Centralized
All requests whether administrative or clinical, HR, etc. come into one place.
Aim for multi-experience intake and then routing to specialized knowledge as needed 
This is often liked due to a more consistent process and UX 

Tiered - often basic, specialist or advanced tiers but these are sometimes also customized

“Hybrid” or blended - Blend of the two and can support both IT, clinical, etc. 

I am also going to provide a few examples of some health systems I have had conversations with and what they did:

Centralized - large health system - with all IT and clinical app issues in one portal/place. Things are then routed to the right team. This move has resulted in better EX and eSAT, but also improved resolution times. 
Tiered - large and growing health system - 65% of issues can be solved in tier 1. They also have recently enhanced automation capabilities and self-service which they believe may also lead to additional improvements. 
Another is more Hybrid in nature but moving to more automation and self-service. They want to reduce call volumes and costs and given the research they conducted, this seems to be the best path forward. 
Another is also Hybrid — IT and clinical apps focused. 

The key is what will work best within your org. I like to point to the attached research about taking an employee-centered approach. I also think our TX research below highlights the importance of your people, too, and using the model that best supports your people and org.

Date: 27-Mar-26
Reference Number: 19325277
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: CISO or Head of Information Security
Purpose: Low/no code workflow automation toolset tailored for cyber engineering teams.
Question Asked: The client is seeking a low/no code workflow automation toolset tailored for cyber engineering teams that bridges the gap between traditional IT automation and security operations automation. Their team is responsible for a broad range of security engineering and cyber engineering tasks and is struggling to find a tool that is flexible and integrated enough to support both IT and security automation use cases. Specifically, the client is looking for a solution that: 

Provides low/no code workflow automation for both IT and security engineering tasks, with strong integration capabilities for a range of security and IT systems.
Can support use cases such as building and configuring virtual security appliances, delivering data pipelines for SOC teams, and automating workflows between systems like ServiceNow, Jira, and security tools (e.g., web proxies).
Acts as a “glue” between disparate security systems and data, enabling automation of both complex and simple tasks.
Analyst Name: Andrew Davies
Discussion Summary: Recommendations
1. Focus on Process and Methodology Before Tools

Prioritize building a clear methodology for automation, using a DevSecOps mindset. Break down manual tasks into repeatable, well-documented processes (the “if/then/else” logic).
Develop a use case library to clearly define what needs to be automated and the steps involved, independent of any specific tool.

2. Lower the Bar for Automation Adoption

Aim for solutions that enable non-expert team members to contribute to automation. Avoid platforms that require deep coding skills for every task.
Use tools or platforms that allow for reusable libraries (e.g., drag-and-drop or low-code/no-code approaches).

3. Evaluate Tools with Proof of Value

Shortlist vendors (e.g., Tines, Swimlane, D3) that offer low-code/no-code workflow automation, but require them to demonstrate solutions to your hardest, most manual use cases.
In proofs of concept, insist vendors show exactly how much manual scripting or custom code is required beyond what’s available “out of the box.”
Assess how much professional services time is needed to get started and how maintainable the solution is after vendor involvement ends.

4. Plan for Legacy and Modern Systems

Recognize that a hybrid environment (legacy and modern systems) will always need “glue” solutions. No single platform will cover 100% of needs, especially with older, non-API systems.
Where possible, use automation tools that can trigger scripts or integrate with legacy systems, but be realistic about what can and cannot be automated.

5. Track and Quantify Current Manual Effort

Begin tracking how much time and effort is spent on manual tasks today (e.g., data preparation, reporting, ticket creation).
Use this data to build a business case for automation, showing potential time and cost savings, and to prioritize automation efforts.

6. Prepare for Organizational Change

Ensure the whole team understands the new processes and document them clearly.
Lower the technical barrier so more staff can participate in automation, not just the most technical engineers.
Plan for ongoing validation and maintenance of automated workflows.

7. Use RFI/RFP to Control Vendor Engagement

When engaging vendors, use a structured RFI/RFP to ensure they address your real requirements, not just deliver generic sales pitches.
Score vendors on how well they meet your specific use cases and requirements.


Next Steps


Document Use Cases and Processes

Finalize and expand your use case library, focusing on the most time-consuming and error-prone manual tasks.
Map out the “if/then/else” logic for each use case.



Track Manual Effort

For the next few weeks, have the team log time spent on key manual processes (e.g., data extraction, transformation, reporting).
Quantify the cost and cognitive load of these tasks.



Develop Requirements for Tool Evaluation

Draft an RFI/RFP document listing your requirements, including:

Ability to automate both modern and legacy systems.
Minimal manual scripting needed.
Ease of use for non-experts.
Maintenance and support model.
Professional services involvement.
Integration with existing tools (e.g., Sentinel, ServiceNow, Jira).





Shortlist and Engage Vendors

Approach Tines, Swimlane, and D3 for demonstrations and proofs of concept.
Provide them with your hardest use cases and require them to show working solutions.
Score each vendor using your RFI/RFP during presentations.



Assess Internal Skills and Training Needs

Identify automation champions in your team.
Plan for training or upskilling as needed to ensure broader adoption.



Plan for Ongoing Validation and Maintenance

Define how automated workflows will be validated, maintained, and updated over time.
Ensure knowledge transfer from any vendor professional services to your team.



Build the Business Case

Use tracked man

Analyst Name: Hiroyuki Katayama
Discussion Summary: 類似インクを他でも出している。一つはITコスト最適化、今回は予算の未消化の話。部門の中で可視化して、責任を持ってもらう。なるべく消化してもらう、消化できなければ早めに返してもらう。そういうことを考えている。ITコスト全体を管理。急にビジネス案件が出拠点ができることがありITコストが増える。ところが突然なくなることもある。これは事前に見えない。バッファーの持ち方。Apptioも検討、だが高い。ITKMDと比較すると自社の数値が大きすぎる。事業に持たせると乱暴な使い方になる
→
ITコスト管理はできるだけ本社側で集約化し、チャージバックで事業側に負担させる。コスト最適化にはこの体制がベスト。ただし、意思決定スピード（案件の優先順位付けなど）が遅くなるケースがあるので、本社ITと事業（地域ごとなど）の間に仲介役（優先順位付けのための委員会、投資評価委員会、事業部の代表も入れる）を入れて、管理する。バッファーは、事業ごとや案件ごとに持つのではなく、本社IT予算全体で持つ、突然大きい予算が必要な時は、財務部門とも交渉して、IT予算以外の事業予算からのバッファーも活用できるよう交渉する）。IT予算のバッファーはおよそ10-15%が一般的。ツールは下記を簡単に説明。ApptioはOpexのXX%で年間のクラウド利用料を決めている。ベンチマーク数値と比較する時は、特定時期にのみ必要とする大きな案件の金額（S4への移行、全社ランサムウェア対策など）は除いた数値で比較する
＊ITFMツールのマーケットガイドMarket Guide for IT Financial Management Tools
＊ANAPLAN：https://www.anaplan.com/jp/：
ファイナンシャル プランニング ソフトウェア、ITコストの予実管理も対象だが、チャージバック機能はないと理解
＊ServiceNow：https://www.servicenow.com/jp/products/it-asset-management.html：
IT資産管理ツール。計算機能が弱いとユーザーからコメントをもらうことが多い。コスト配賦／チャージバック機能はないとの理解。一部企業は不足機能をアドオンで開発していたり、ServiceNowでコスト管理していると言っていた企業がApptioを購入したりしている

Client Question
I am reaching out to ask for your assistance in finding leading solutions for managing employee-facing content. Currently, our content is spread across various platforms, including the portal, Adobe, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and a few special solutions like Quadient. This dispersed approach can sometimes lead to inconsistencies and inefficiencies.

***Updated scope:
The client indicated that the note below has parts of what he is looking for so if you could get an analyst to speak to this note as a starting point that would be great.

Content Services Strategy: Through the Lens of Total Experience

Gartner Response
Using the definition of employee content experiences in Content Services Strategy: Through the Lens of Total Experience, these include content collaboration for the digital workplace (ie. Microsoft OneDrive, GoogleDrive), search and AI assistants for the digital workplace (ie. Microsoft 365 Search and Copilot, Google Workspace with Gemini), and intranet packaged solutions (ie. Simpplr). We distinguish between general-purpose content experience for employees from operational content experiences for employees in their professional personas and role (ie. finance, customer service, IT, supply chain, and HR).

It is common for content to be distributed across operational systems like SalesForce and ServiceNow. For example, Salesforce might be the system of record for purchase order and contracts. ServiceNow might hold customer service queries and knowledge bases. However, operational systems like Salesforce and ServiceNow have very weak document management capabilities. For that reason, they are often integrated with operational document management platforms like OpenText Content Management, Hyland Onbase, and Microsoft Sharepoint).

Adobe Experience Management (AEM) is used to support content for customer experiences as a Digital Experience Platform (DXP). Quadient, a customer communications management (CCM) tool, is designed to generate customer content like statements and letters. Both Adobe Experience Manager and Quadient are examples of content services supporting the customer experience.

Without knowing more about your situation it’s difficult to advise you on where to focus. See below further research more focussed on content for the employee experience.

Solution Path for Document Management in Microsoft 365 
Magic Quadrant for Document Management 
Magic Quadrant for Intranet Packaged Solutions 
Quick Answer: How to Assess Intranet Technology? 
Key Considerations for Microsoft 365-Based Intranets
Modernize Employee Communications for Enhanced Digital Experiences 

I suggest you schedule a follow-up call and we can discuss your situation in depth and I can then give you more targeted advice.

Reference Number: 19276441

Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: Sent to the client after the call:

Prioritize excellence over expansion. Even during an RFP, reliable return will come from tightening health rules, alerts, and dashboards on what you already run. Tool and data sprawl is a barrier to genuine value.

Keep ThousandEyes where it continues adding practical value. Its strengths in path visualization, BGP and DNS context, and distributed vantage points complement traditional monitoring approaches and help close visibility gaps around internet and SaaS dependencies.

Run observability as a platform service with a centralized team. Centralized ownership reduces tool proliferation and creates more consistent telemetry practices.

Increase the depth of your ServiceNow integrations. If possible, bring events into ServiceNow ITOM for correlation, incident creation, and guided workflows to help standardize response and reduce manual triage time.

Continue strengthening your OTel strategy. OTel is the vendor‑neutral standard for portable metrics, logs, and traces, with strong community backing and expanding semantic conventions that support multicloud and hybrid environments.

Use telemetry pipelines when volume and diversity justify it. In high‑volume environments, a pipeline layer should manage routing, filtering, enrichment, and cost control across multiple tools without forcing architectural lock‑in.

Account for the value of work already invested. Deployments such as agent automation, broad vantage point coverage, and existing data flows remain assets. Moving to pipeline layers and open standards will allow you to carry that work forward even as you evaluate new platforms.

Formalize incident response playbooks with selective automation. Define the workflows around what triggers action, what can be automated safely, and what requires review. ServiceNow‑based automation frameworks help reduce manual effort and improve consistency.

Date: 23-Mar-26
Reference Number: 19390791
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Manufacturing
Buyer Role: Software Engineering - Other Role
Purpose: Identifying and Prioritizing High-Impact AI Use Cases for IT Organizations
Question Asked: What are the most valuable AI use cases for IT organizations aiming to improve efficiency and service delivery? H
How should IT leaders evaluate and prioritize AI initiatives to align with operational goals and resource constraints? 
What leading practices does Gartner recommend for successfully launching and scaling AI within IT, including integration with platforms such as ServiceNow?
Analyst Name: C.A. Swan
Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary

We discussed how to drive AI adoption across, with a focus on the software development lifecycle. The core question centered on where to start with AI tooling and how to mature from assisted AI usage toward more advanced orchestration patterns. The guidance emphasized a methodical, phased approach starting with high-toil development tasks and expanding incrementally, with specific attention to AI-assisted testing as an immediate tactical opportunity.

Key Actions

Start with AI-assisted code generation in the create phase of your SDLC and expand outward from there. Your teams are already coding across multiple languages and platforms, so the quickest wins come from applying AI to the repetitive, high-toil tasks every developer handles: writing boilerplate code, configuration files, documentation and unit tests. Use your primary AI coding tool for these tasks first and let teams build comfort and fluency before expanding into other lifecycle phases.

Make AI-assisted testing your first major tactical initiative. You previously stood down a dedicated testing team, and your current teams are carrying testing responsibilities across large, complex enterprise programs. AI tools integrated into your existing development environments can generate test cases, expand test coverage and validate configurations across your diverse technology stack, whether that involves ServiceNow, PowerShell, .NET or scripting languages. The key is to use AI test generation within the same toolchain your developers already work in rather than standing up a separate testing infrastructure. Your developers write the implementation, then prompt AI to generate corresponding test coverage, review the output and iterate. This approach fills the gap left by the disbanded testing team without requiring a dedicated headcount investment.

Adopt AI tools incrementally rather than deploying multiple tools at once. Each AI tool introduces its own behaviors and learning curve, and turning on several simultaneously creates chaos rather than productivity gains. Stay with your primary tool until you identify specific quality gaps, then bring in a specialized tool to address that gap. Code review is a common first area where organizations outgrow their general-purpose AI tool and benefit from a specialized alternative.

Extend AI assistance beyond the create phase into observability and incident triage once your teams are comfortable with code generation. Connect your AI platform to your monitoring tools so that when alerts fire, AI can enrich the incident context with relevant information before a human triages it. This reduces time-to-resolution without requiring changes to your existing monitoring stack.

Stay in the assisted AI paradigm for now. The jump from AI-as-assistant to AI-as-orchestrator requires significant organizational restructuring, upskilling and new governance models. Your organization will get reliable productivity gains in the 15 to 25% range from assisted AI adoption alone. Moving to agentic orchestration prematurely introduces risks that outweigh the incremental benefits, particularly for a large shared services organization where stability and consistency matter. Build the assisted foundation first, measure your results and make the orchestration decision when your teams have the maturity and resources to support it.

Discussion Summary: You need to think about migration not only in the specific functionality of Rally/Jira but what your overall environment and toolchain look like.  The reference architecture below can help with framing this.
Jira is very flexible in how it is used and like most developer tools it is shaped by how Atlassian works internally vs. external thought providers.  IE the features/functions are driven by how Atlassian things about development (and input from customers) not Person X has come up with a framework, and we are going to support that one.  The note on Software Engineering at Atlassian will help describe that
Jira comes in different flavors: Jira (which also comes in different levels: Std, Premium, Enterprise) is the core edition oriented at “anyone”, Jira Product Discovery is oriented at Product Managers and the work that is upstream of putting things into the development planning process, Jira Align is oriented at the management layer in a SAFe oriented organization(other frameworks are also supported) and it “includes” seats for Jira.  There are questions about will Align continue to exist and certainly Atlassian has been moving functionality around etc. as they mature, kind of like ServiceNow has done as features appear in the marketplace then are put into specific editions or new products.  
I don’t see a lot of new SAFe competitors in the market.  The Market Guide we produced last year is still relevant, below is a link to the document produced by looking at our Peer Insights feedback about enterprise agile tools.  What we do see new tools are tools to replace Jira and a focus on “team level” agile rather than scaled.  Like Jira itself these can generally be configured to support specific frameworks, they just don’t take an opinionated direction: Linear, Shortcut, Plane.so are all examples.  All of these companies are like Atlassian several years ago: direct web sales, freemium models etc.  
You must also consider AI's role and how it will change things over the next 5 years.  Agentic AI is now making tools like Jira almost an “IDE” you work with an agent to plan, design, create and manage stories, tests, and code.  We see in very early adopters the concept of a shift from the AWS 2 Pizza team to the 2 Person team.  I think this will also then impact how we manage, monitor etc.

Discussion Summary: To: Danny Asaoka, UNIV OF CA IRVINE HEALTH 
From: Roger Benn, Gartner 
Inquiry reference: 19204775 
Client question: Requesting written response from Roger Benn as a f/u to inquiry 19103194. Requesting information that was discussed on the call for additional PMO specific follow up as a written response as the client explores vendors and priority use-cases to streamline intake operations with UI Path. 

Dear Danny Asaoka: 

Post Integration Reality and Financial Pressure
Most $2–5B revenue AMCs now entering AI and automation discussions are doing so from a position of operational fragility rather than growth. Recent market signals underscore this reality. Over 30% of announced U.S. hospital transactions in 2024 involved at least one financially distressed party, and several high-profile integrations have failed to deliver anticipated synergies
For AMCs that have recently integrated new hospitals, “integration completion” often masks:
•	Duplicate ERP systems
•	Multiple Epic instances or configurations
•	Inconsistent intake, registration, and scheduling workflows

Implication for vendor discussions:
Every automation or AI proposal must be evaluated through an in year cash impact lens. Platforms that cannot credibly demonstrate measurable cost reduction, capacity release, or revenue acceleration within 6–12 months should be deprioritized.

Intake Operations as a Priority Use Case for Automation
Intake Is a High Return Starting Point
Across Providers and AMCs, patient intake (referral intake, scheduling, registration, and prior authorization) consistently emerges as one of the highest ROI operational automation domains. Intake workflows are:
•	Labor-intensive
•	Highly variable across departments
•	A frequent source of downstream Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) leakage
Gartner research and market observations show that automating intake improves throughput, reduces abandoned referrals, and increases downstream clean claims rates when implemented correctly (Notable Health, 2025; ServiceNow, 2025).

 “Build vs. Buy” Considerations in Intake Automation
Historically, many AMCs attempted to automate intake processes by building custom Robotic Process Automation (RPA) bots using platforms such as UiPath or Automation Anywhere. This approach is increasingly unsustainable.
Observed challenges include:
•	High maintenance burden when payer portals, Epic workflows, or forms change
•	Fragile screen scraping and Optical Character Recognition (OCR) dependencies
•	Slow time to value (often 6–9 months)
Market shift:
Providers are moving toward vertical intelligence vendors (for example, Notable Health and Waystar) that sell outcome-based solutions such as “Automated Intake” or “Prior Authorization,” maintaining payer logic and integrations at their cost (Blueprint Systems, 2025; Notable Health, 2025).

UiPath: Where It Fits—and Where It Does Not
Appropriate UiPath Use Cases
UiPath remains a strong choice for unattended back-office automation where processes are:
•	Rules-driven
•	Internally controlled
•	Not deeply dependent on payer or clinical logic
Common AMC use cases where UiPath performs well include:
•	Finance close and reconciliations
•	Supply chain exceptions handling
•	Human Resources (HR) onboarding and offboarding
UiPath’s governance, audit logging, and role-based access controls are comparatively mature, which is critical in a federated AMC environment (UiPath, 2025).

UiPath Risks for Intake and RCM Workflows
UiPath is not well-positioned as the primary engine for clinical intake or RCM automation due to:
•	The “maintenance tax” associated with constantly changing payer portals
•	Fragility introduced by screen-based automation
•	Epic Hyperdrive migration risk (see Section 5)
Guidance for UiPath discussions:
•	Position UiPath as a supporting platform for finance and enterprise operations
•	Avoid committing UiPath to net-new intake or c

The core concept is to stop relying purely on theoretical, top-down data models and instead integrate data products, the Y-diagram, data architecture, and system physics into a unified, observability-driven ecosystem.

These four elements converge to guide a modern knowledge graph strategy.

1. Data Architecture as the Observability Foundation (Data Fabric)
•	Modern data architecture dictates that a knowledge graph should not be built from scratch via human interviews; it should emerge organically from a Data Fabric.
•	Active Metadata as Triples: A Data Fabric acts as an observability engine that continuously analyzes the "exhaust" of your systems, such as query logs, access pathways, and processing code. Because metadata is inherently composed of Subject-Predicate-Object triples, parsing this code automatically generates the nodes and edges required to populate a knowledge graph.

Data Management Inversion: By observing these real-world operations, the architecture learns how data is actually utilized rather than how it was designed to be utilized.  The knowledge graph becomes an empirical map of enterprise data behavior, which provides the necessary intelligence to support the delivery layer.

2. The Y-Diagram for Designing Reusable Data Products (Data Mesh)
•	While the Data Fabric observes and maps the data, the Data Mesh serves as the delivery framework to present these insights as Data Products
•	The knowledge graph requires these products to be highly disciplined to prevent chaos.
•	Preventing Proliferation: A major failure in modern architecture is "data product proliferation," which occurs when Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) build highly isolated, single-use data products based entirely on their specific business use cases.
•	The Y-Diagram: To prevent this, the knowledge graph must enforce the "lowercase y" diagram logic. This mandates that a true, reusable data product exists only at the intersection of Data Objects (consistent groupings of attributes, the bottom of the "y"), Governance (quality plus access rights, the top right of the "y"), and Use Cases (the top left of the "y").

Subordinating the Use Case: The Y-diagram explicitly dictates that the Use Case must be subordinated to the intersection of Governance and Data Objects. The knowledge graph uses this rule to identify redundant use-case efforts and recommend consolidating them into governed, reusable data products.

3. Applying the Laws of Data Physics (Resource Asset Allocation)
A modernized knowledge graph strategy must account for the four laws of data management physics—CPU, Memory, Storage, and I/O-Network bandwidth.
•	The graph cannot simply connect all data logically; it must evaluate if those connections are physically viable.
•	Predictability vs. Volatility: By using the knowledge graph to analyze run-time statistics, the system determines the predictability of data usage.
•	If the graph shows that a data product's usage is highly predictable, physics dictates that the data should be physically stored (e.g., in a data warehouse or lakehouse) to optimize CPU and memory costs.

Separating Logic and Physics: When the logical business requirements of the data product diverge from the physical capabilities of the system (e.g., trying to force massive volumes of data through a constrained network "garden hose"), the knowledge graph signals the architecture to introduce a semantic interpreter or data virtualization layer to bridge the gap without moving the physical data.

Analyst Name: Robert Stoneman
Discussion Summary: Governments are using emerging tech to address managing vehicle licenses. This includes blockchain/distributed ledger platforms for titles and lifecycle records, and mobile/wallet-based digital registration and ownership credentials. For full disclosure, the names of vendors mentioned as part of the below does not mean Gartner recommends these vendors for your own initiatives. They are for descriptive purposes only.

Digital vehicle transfer solutions implemented in various countries

Detran-SP – Digital Vehicle Transfer (TDV):

The best example I am aware of comes from a sister organization in Brazil. They submitted their TDV initiative to the 2024 Gartner Eye on Innovation Awards for Government, winning in the Americas region. I have included a one slide overview below.

 

Based on some further information, I have expanded on this below.

•	Aims and Outcomes: The primary aim of the TDV initiative was to digitize and transform a traditionally slow, costly, and bureaucratic system that relied on manual processes, paper validation, and an average processing time of over ten days. By eliminating the need for queues, notary services, and travel to service centers, it has reduced the process duration to approximately 5 minutes (with a record time of 19 seconds).

•	Pre-requisites: To use the service, both the buyer and the seller must hold a “Silver” or “Gold” authentication seal on gov.br. They must also install the Poupatempo app on their phones. The vehicle must also possess a digital Certificado de Registro de Veículo (CRV), or a paper one that has been converted into a legally valid electronic format at a notary. A vehicle identification inspection must have also been completed within the previous 60 days.

•	Citizen facing experience: 

o	For sellers, the app automatically checks if all pre-requisites are met and utilizes AI-driven facial recognition to securely confirm the seller's identity. 
o	The seller inputs the buyer's details, confirms the sale information, and generates the ATPVe (Authorization for Transfer of Vehicle Ownership). 
o	From the buyers perspective, they undergo the same identification process, confirm the transaction data, provide a self-declaration of address, and sign electronically. 
o	Once the buyer confirms their intent, the seller returns to the app to verify the final details and applies their own electronic signature. 
o	The buyer pays the transfer fee directly within the app (using Pix via a QR code). 
o	Upon payment confirmation, the transfer is instantly validated, and the new digital document is made available in the buyer's digital traffic wallet app. 

•	Underlying technology stack: The entire operation relies on Red Hat APIs, RPA for mainframe automation, ServiceNow automation, and blockchain to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and security of the collected data. The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) is involved in the biometric validation. The State Department of Finance is also involved to enable the Pix payment platform. 

California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV):

This uses smart contracts that model title transfer workflows, including escrow and DMV checks. To the best of my knowledge, this is not yet running as the authoritative system of record (which is a sensible approach while it is being adopted), though it has been expanded to a state-wide production solution.

It has developed over two phases.

•	Pilot phase: In 2023, the California DMV engaged Oxhead Alpha to build a “shadow ledger” (a blockchain mirror of DMV title records) running on a private Tezos blockchain testnet. 

•	Rollout phase: In July 2024, this progressed to a broader rollout using different infrastructure. The DMV, in partnership with Oxhead Alpha and Ava Labs, digitized 42 million car titles onto a permissioned Avalanche Subnet (a private, DMV-run version of the blockchain).

Rns Sent:
Universal Orchestrator — Governing AI Agents, Bots, and Humans at Scale
Emerging Tech: AI Vendor Race: Enterprise AI Will Fail to Scale Without Agentic Orchestration Platforms
AI Factory Layer from Soyeb
Analyst Name: Saikat Ray
Discussion Summary: What Changes with Agentic Automation?
Agentic automation introduces smart, goal-driven systems capable of interpreting intent, planning actions, and dynamically choosing the best resources—be they APIs, human input, or RPA bots. The major shift is in control: instead of fixed, end-to-end scripts, these agents decide which steps to take, handling exceptions by involving people when necessary. This moves automation from task completion to achieving real business outcomes.
Role of RPA
RPA remains essential as the most secure and reliable way to interface with legacy systems, enterprise apps, and engineering tools. Bots continue to log in, move data, enforce rules, and keep audit trails.
Implications for the Airbus Automation Factory
The automation factory's role is expanding. Previously centered on bot development and management, it is evolving into a broader capability hub for automation. The focus shifts from simply the number of bots deployed to the number of business outcomes delivered reliably and autonomously. New roles are emerging around agent design, orchestration, and governance, while bot development expertise continues to be valuable.
UiPath’s Position
UiPath is not replaced in this model; rather, it becomes the execution engine that agentic systems rely upon. UiPath’s strengths in governance and auditability remain critical, especially for regulated industries like aerospace. However, for multi-agent collaboration and advanced planning, higher-level orchestration solutions will complement UiPath.
Next Steps for Adoption
Transitioning safely means not disrupting existing RPA bots. It's best to begin with complex, exception-prone processes where current automation struggles—such as incident triage, maintenance documentation, procurement exceptions, and engineering change analysis. Here, agentic systems handle decisions while bots execute actions, layering intelligence atop proven automation.

Key Takeaway for AI Agent Orchestration

AI agent orchestration is rapidly evolving into a strategic architecture decision that determines where enterprise execution authority resides. A well-defined orchestration authority drives who persists workflow state, manages exceptions, coordinates human-in-the-loop controls, and produces authoritative audit evidence.

•	Prioritize dominant AI agent orchestration patterns (workflow, structural and specialized) before evaluating platforms.
•	Define enterprise control-plane placement across systems of record, system of intelligence and system of action.
•	Recognize that no single platform category dominates across all dimensions; orchestration strategy will be typically hybrid.
•	Align orchestration selection to long-term governance, operating model, scalability and cost sustainability — not short-term innovation velocity.


No single orchestration category can serve all agentic use cases. AI Agent orchestration is a technology portfolio architecture decision — not a single-platform selection.

Date: 22-Jan-26
Reference Number: 19221054
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Energy and Utilities
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architecture - Other Role
Purpose: WR - Review of Observability Maturity Assessment (follow up to 19162895)
Question Asked: Present a written response, including specific technical, process, and organizational recommendations. The team will then discusses feedback, clarifies points, and agrees on next steps.
Analyst Name: Martin Caren
Discussion Summary: Thank you for your inquiry.

I am pleased to elaborate on your inquiry with this written response, and to provide further assistance as you progress with your work, as needed. Here is my assessment:

Executive Summary
Your organization is at a pivotal moment, transitioning from legacy, reactive operations to a more modern, proactive, and integrated IT operations model. The assessment and conversations have surfaced both strengths (a clear understanding of current pain points and a willingness to modernize) and gaps (notably in change management, process clarity, and cross-team collaboration). Below are targeted recommendations across technical, process, and organizational dimensions.

________________________________________
1. Technical Recommendations
A. Observability Platform & Tool Rationalization
•	Reduce Tool Sprawl: Inventory all monitoring and observability tools. Identify overlaps and redundancies, then consolidate to a core set of platforms that cover servers, network, storage, applications, and cloud.
•	Golden Signals: Implement the “Four Golden Signals” (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) for all business-critical applications, not just a select few. This should be a minimum baseline for all services, considering your culture of high availability.
•	Unified Data Ingestion: Ensure logs, metrics, and traces from all layers (network, server, storage, application, load balancers, etc.) are ingested into a central observability platform. This enables correlation and root cause analysis.
•	Synthetic Monitoring: Standardize on synthetic checks for key user-facing services, but avoid duplication (e.g., if load balancer health checks are sufficient, don’t duplicate with synthetics unless there’s a gap).
•	Automated Alert Tuning: Implement noise reduction strategies—alert deduplication, dynamic thresholds, and event correlation—to address alert fatigue and ensure critical events are actionable.
B. Integration with ITSM
•	Integrate observability tools with your IT Service Management (ITSM) platform (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira) for automated ticket creation, enrichment, and escalation.
________________________________________
2. Process Recommendations
A. Incident, Problem, and Change Management
•	Formalize Ownership: Clearly define owners for Incident, Problem, and Change Management processes. These should be roles with accountability, not ad-hoc assignments.
•	Cross-Functional War Rooms: For P1/major incidents, establish a documented protocol for convening all relevant teams immediately (network, server, storage, application, etc.)—not sequentially.
•	Post-Incident Reviews: Mandate blameless post-incident reviews (PIRs/RCA) for all major incidents. Use these to identify process, tooling, and communication gaps.
•	Onboarding and Offboarding: Establish a process for onboarding new applications/services into observability (instrumentation, alerting, runbooks) and for decommissioning obsolete ones.
B. Change Management (Organizational Change)
•	Change Champions: Appoint “change champions” in each team to advocate for and drive adoption of new processes and tools.
•	Training & Enablement: Provide targeted training for staff on new observability tools, processes, and cross-team workflows.
•	Feedback Loops: Set up regular feedback sessions to capture what’s working and what isn’t, and iterate accordingly.
C. Metric-Driven Improvement
•	MTTR/MTTI Tracking: Track Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) and Mean Time to Identify (MTTI) for incidents. Use these as KPIs for process improvement.
•	Coverage Gaps: Regularly review monitoring coverage against a prioritized list of business-critical services.
________________________________________
3. Organizational Recommendations
A. Governance & Sponsorship
•	Executive Sponsorship: Secure ongoing executive sponsorship for the transformation. This ensures prioritization and resource allocation.
•	Steering Committee

Date: 25-Mar-26
Reference Number: 19423033
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: Infrastructure Security
Purpose: Data Retention Refactoring
Question Asked: Lorin Ball is interested in refactoring their data retention policy to simplify and standardize retention periods. They aim to establish a default retention period, such as seven years, with exceptions based on regulatory requirements. 
Is there a standard record retention period used throughout the financial services industry?
7 Years is the standard that we believe can be applied, is that what they are seeing with other clients?
We believe there would be exceptions for state level regs - specifically for collections data/other items I haven't thought of.
Analyst Name: Apurva Singh
Discussion Summary: Retention Model Design
•     There is no single industry-standard retention period; leading institutions adopt a baseline (commonly 5–7 years) with structured exceptions, rather than a universal rule.
•     A 7-year default is viable as an enterprise baseline for core financial records, but should not be applied uniformly across all customer data.
•     The effectiveness of the model depends on standardizing the decision framework (default + exceptions + triggers) rather than standardizing a single duration.
•     Over-applying a uniform retention period increases privacy risk, storage cost, and eDiscovery burden, particularly for short-lived or non-regulatory data.


Exception Management Approach
•     Exceptions should follow a “burden of proof” model, where the business must demonstrate legal, regulatory, or material justification for deviation.
•     Establish a centralized exception governance model to avoid fragmentation, exceptions should not be defined or approved by individual data owners.
•     Use a predefined exception taxonomy (e.g., collections, legal hold, fraud, state-specific requirements) to control scope and prevent ad hoc proliferation.


Governance and Accountability
•     Assign a single accountable approver for exceptions within the Legal function, with Compliance and Records Management acting as co-reviewers.
•     Position data stewards as requestors and owners of exceptions, responsible for justification and scope, but not approval.
•     Maintain clear separation between decision authority (Legal/Compliance) and execution (IT/platform teams) to ensure consistency and defensibility.


Tooling and Implementation (Microsoft 365 E5 / Purview)
•     Use Microsoft Purview as the enforcement layer through retention policies, labels, records management, and legal holds.
•     Manage exceptions through retention labels and legal holds, which override default policies at the data level.
•     Recognize that Purview tracks exceptions implicitly (labels, holds, audit logs) but does not provide a full governance lifecycle view.
•     Implement a central exception register (e.g., ServiceNow or GRC tool) to track justification, ownership, approval, and review cycles alongside Purview enforcement.


Discovery and Policy Initialization
•     Begin with a targeted discovery focused on high-risk domains (customer and collections data) rather than enterprise-wide scope.
•     Identify minimum required retention (“minimum needs”) instead of business-preferred retention to avoid over-retention.
•     Use discovery outputs to define the initial baseline and exception categories, then expand iteratively.
•     Establish cross-functional alignment (Legal, Compliance, IT, Records) early to ensure consistent regulatory interpretation and avoid rework.

How Power Apps and Power Automate are evolving for complex enterprise use cases
Power Apps
Power Apps is evolving from a low‑code app builder into an AI‑augmented, enterprise application platform.
Key directions include:
Embedded Copilot and agents inside apps
Copilot chat and task‑oriented agents are being embedded directly into model‑driven apps so users can ask questions, generate insights, and trigger actions without leaving the application context.
Human‑in‑the‑loop agent governance
New agent supervision experiences such as agent feeds and approval workflows allow enterprises to monitor, approve, and audit agent actions. This is critical for regulated and higher‑risk business processes.
Enterprise app composition
Power Apps is moving toward solution‑level design where apps, agents, workflows, and analytics are created together, not as isolated artifacts. This supports larger, cross‑functional business scenarios.
Improved lifecycle controls
Offline profiles, notifications, environment separation, and managed environments continue to improve to support frontline and mission‑critical apps at scale.

________________________________________
Power Automate
Power Automate is shifting from task automation to end‑to‑end process orchestration.
Key directions include:
AI‑first automation
Generative actions, intelligent document processing, and adaptive flows reduce the need for rigid rule‑based logic and allow automations to handle variability.
Process‑level visibility and observability
Automation Center, process maps, and ROI analytics provide enterprise teams with visibility into how automations perform across cloud flows, desktop flows, and departments.
Human‑in‑the‑loop as a standard pattern
Advanced approvals, exception handling, and escalation paths are becoming first‑class capabilities for enterprise workflows.
Closer integration with apps and agents
Power Automate flows are increasingly designed to be triggered by apps, Copilot Studio agents, and Dataverse events as part of a broader solution.

________________________________________
Expansion of connectors and integrations
Connector ecosystem
Microsoft continues to expand and modernize the connector ecosystem:
Native OpenAPI v3 support
Custom connectors can now be built directly from modern OpenAPI v3 specifications, reducing friction with enterprise and developer‑built APIs.
Agent‑ready connectors
Microsoft now supports connectors specifically designed to be safely consumed by Copilot Studio agents, including certification and publishing paths for ISVs.
Ongoing catalog growth
Microsoft and partners continue to add and enhance connectors across SaaS platforms, infrastructure tools, and industry systems.
Why it matters
Enterprises can integrate Power Platform solutions with developer‑managed systems without maintaining parallel integration technology stacks.


………...

A better point of comparison is at the process or activity level. Some HR Service Management solutions offer this level of benchmarking (e.g. ServiceNow, ZenDesk, Workday), though it is limited or a newly added feature for most.

What does the return to sender % look like where colleagues continue to respond to the same case – we have 3% want to understand what other companies use.
This is not a commonly tracked and targeted metric in most HR service teams. Where I do see HR teams tracking this, it is often to inform quality assurance actions and support individual performance. The guidance from our Customer Support experts is to measure and use the Trend of Cases Reopened as follows:

•	Definition: Tracks the number and percentage of service cases that are reopened after initial closure, indicating unresolved issues.
•	Calculation: (Number of cases reopened/total cases closed) × 100.
•	Reporting Frequency: Weekly trend analysis.
•	Target: ≤ 5% of cases reopened.
•	Actionable Use: An upward trend in reopened cases should prompt investigation and corrective action to address recurring problems and reduce customer effort.


What other quality measures do companies use and what are the best-in-class measures?
HR Service measures are varied in use and application. I recommend aligning your metrics and reporting strategy to Value Stories to communicate impact and value contribution aligned to what the organization prioritizes.

Use these value stories to clearly demonstrate the value of the HR function to the executive audience. The best HR scorecards are built around two or three value stories. These stories help the business understand the HR function’s ambitions to support business objectives and the function’s progress toward doing so. 

See examples from:
•	Scalable Recruiting Operations Support Team (Gallagher) – cycle time, recruiter time saved, ticket volumes, SLA attainment, error rate, CSAT, contribution to enhancements
•	People Operations Team (Discovery Limited) – CSAT, SLA attainment, ticket volumes, cycle time, process automation, HR efficiency rate
•	Expansion of HR Operations to Drive Strategic Impact (HPE) – HEART measures, CSAT, unique contacts, return contacts, ticket volume 

What is the best-in-class time to hire from Post Offer to Onboard?
We don’t measure this explicitly. It could be inferred from our benchmarks on Time to Fill based on the delta between Time to offer Acceptance and Time to Start. This is not very useful as an external benchmark however, as there are so many context factors that can influence which are not reflective of process efficiency (e.g. notice periods, pre-boarding requirements, custom, garden leave requirements, etc.).

How long do background checks take from vendors by region and by country?
This is not a solution market that Gartner covers. We do not have any benchmark data or research on this topic.

What is the % of late terminations that other companies have and what is a best-in-class number?
We do not have any benchmark data or research on this topic.

What is the general CSAT for onboarding that colleague provide by region after 6 months on the job? What is the same number for one week on the job?
